content_html:
Transformer Processing ↔ Human Memory

Encoding, Attention, Reconstruction, Context, Prediction

Transformers don’t “store” verbatim memories, and humans don’t “replay” them. Both systems reconstruct content from distributed representations under attention and context constraints.

Transformer Processing Human Memory
Encoding
text → tokens → IDs → embeddings → contextual vectors via self‑attention.		 Encoding
sensory input → features → distributed neural codes; traces form via synaptic plasticity.
Representation
distributed; no single neuron/token stores “the meaning.”		 Representation
distributed across cortical networks; no single “memory cell” holds an episode.
Attention
self‑attention weights context‑relevant tokens dynamically.		 Attention
fronto‑parietal and salience networks prioritise signals; working memory gates detail.
Retrieval/Generation
predicts next token from context (probabilistic reconstruction).		 Recall
reconstructive; reactivation of traces + schemas/emotion; vulnerable to bias/confabulation.
Context dependence
meaning of a token changes with neighbours and prompts.		 Context dependence
cues, mood, goals reshape recall content and confidence.
Learning objective
next‑token prediction; captures statistical structure.		 Evolutionary objective
next‑event prediction; memory supports anticipation and action.
Limits
finite context window; no persistent episodic memory unless augmented.		 Limits
capacity/decay; interference; reconstruction errors (“seven sins”).

The analogy is structural, not literal. Transformers are engineered predictors; human memory is biological and goal‑directed — both lean on distributed codes, attention, and context‑dependent reconstruction.
